note: A way of telling the time by the stars. The sun is in the constellation Aries. Taurus, the next sign, now stands at the highest point of the sky, where the sun stood at noon. So it is about two in the afternoon.
Scorpio is the sign opposite Taurus. On the other side of the earth, at Jerusalem, it stands at the midnight point of the sky: there it is about two in the morning.
The stair cut in the rock from the sixth terrace, of gluttony, to the seventh and last, of lust.
One of Dante's many similes from watching birds. He wants to ask a question and is afraid to trouble his guides, who are climbing fast.

context: He begins the answer with two comparisons, then hands the question to Statius.

note: The question left hanging since Canto 23. The gluttons are shades. They have no bodies and need no food, yet they are starved to the bone. How?

A hero in Ovid's Metamorphoses. At his birth the Fates decreed he would live only as long as a log then burning on the hearth. His mother pulled it from the fire and hid it. Years later he killed her brothers, and in her rage she threw it back. As the log burned, he wasted away and died. Virgil's point: a body can be consumed by a cause that has nothing to do with food.
The second comparison. A reflection moves with every movement of the person in front of the glass. In the same way, the visible form of a shade shows whatever its soul is feeling.

context: Why Virgil gives way to him is debated. The usual answer is that the explanation ends in a truth of faith, God's creation of each human soul, which a Christian is better placed to teach.

note: To answer, Statius goes back to the beginning: how a human being is conceived, how the soul comes to it, and what the soul does at death. The science is Aristotle's, as taught in the universities of Dante's day, above all by Thomas Aquinas.

In medieval physiology, food is refined step by step into blood, which feeds the body. A small part, the most refined, is not used up. In the heart it receives the power to shape a whole new body, and it becomes the father's seed.
The male sexual organs. Statius is being modest.
The mother's blood in the womb, "nature's vessel". Aristotle taught that the mother supplies the material of the child and the father's seed supplies the shaping power. The female egg was unknown.

quote: one meant to be passive, one active
note: The mother's blood is the matter that is worked on. The father's seed does the work, because it comes from the heart, the "perfect place".
The first stage. The embryo has what Aristotle called a vegetative soul: it is alive, feeds and grows, as a plant does. But a plant has reached its goal, and the embryo is only beginning.
The second stage: the soul of an animal, with movement and sensation.

Dante's word is "sea fungus": a sponge, or some such simple sea creature, which was thought to move and feel though it has no distinct organs. The embryo is like that for a while, and then begins to form organs for each of its powers.
The hard point. Dante's word for "human" here means a speaking being. Growth and feeling can come from the parents. Reason cannot.

context: He taught that the power of understanding is not part of each person's soul. It is a single intellect, apart from all bodies and shared by all mankind. If that were so, no individual soul would survive death. Christian thinkers, Aquinas among them, fought the idea hard.

note: A term of medieval philosophy: the mind's capacity to take in ideas and understand, called "possible" because it can become any thought.
Sight has the eye and hearing the ear, but no part of the body does the thinking. From this Averroes concluded that the intellect is not the body's own.
God, in Aristotle's phrase: the first cause of all motion in the universe.
As God breathed the breath of life into Adam (Genesis 2:7). The rational soul does not come from the parents. God makes it new for every human being, directly.

The point of the whole speech. A person does not have three souls, one of a plant, one of an animal and one of a mind. The soul God breathes in takes the lower powers into itself and is single. It "reflects upon itself": it knows that it knows.
A comparison for the union. The sun's heat, which is not a material thing, joins with the juice of the grape and the two become one new thing, wine. So God's breath joins with what nature has made.
The one of the three Fates who spins the thread of each life. When her thread runs out, the person dies. Canto 21 used the same image.

The soul takes everything with it. The "human" powers are those of the body, such as growth and the senses, now only potential because they have no organs. The "divine" powers are those of the mind, which need no organ.
The three powers of the mind in Augustine's teaching. Free of the body, they are keener than in life.
The bank of the river Acheron, where the damned gather to be ferried into Hell (Inferno 3), or the mouth of the Tiber, where an angel collects the saved for the voyage to Purgatory (Canto 2).
The same shaping power that built the body in the womb. It has no flesh to work on now, so it works on the air around it.
The rainbow. Wet air takes on colors from the sun's rays, which come from outside it. So the air around the soul takes on a shape from the soul.
A flame goes wherever its fire is carried. The body of air goes wherever the soul goes.

context: Statius explains the word. The soul makes itself a body of air that can be seen, and has organs for every sense. This account is Dante's own blend of ideas and was never Church teaching, but the whole poem depends on it: it is how the dead can be seen, speak, weep and suffer.

note: The answer at last. The airy body shows what the soul feels. The gluttons' souls burn with hunger and thirst, so their shades are gaunt.
The seventh terrace, the highest, where lust is purged. Lust is the least grave of the seven sins in Dante's scheme, a love of something good carried to excess, so it is purged nearest to Heaven.

The contrapasso of the lustful: they burned with desire, and now they walk in fire that burns the desire away. The inner wall throws flame across the terrace and a wind from the edge bends it back, leaving only a narrow path along the drop.

quote: your eyes on a tight rein
note: A warning about the footing, with a second meaning on this terrace. Desire enters by the eyes.
"God of supreme mercy", the opening of a Latin hymn sung in the night office of the Church. It asks God to burn the body with fitting flames, so that it may stay clean of lust.

context: "I know not a man": her answer to the angel Gabriel, who has told her she will bear a son (Luke 1:34). It is the first example of chastity on this terrace.

note: The virgin goddess of the hunt and the moon, who lived in the woods with a band of nymphs sworn to chastity. She is the example from classical myth, set beside Mary.

Another name for Callisto, one of Diana's nymphs. Ovid tells in the Metamorphoses how Jupiter seduced her. When Diana saw that she was pregnant, she drove her out of the band. Juno turned her into a bear, and Jupiter set her in the sky as the Great Bear.
Lust. Venus is the goddess of love.

quote: wives and husbands who were chaste
note: Chastity here does not mean only virginity. Married people who are faithful to each other are chaste too.
The last of the seven P's on Dante's forehead, and the last sin to be healed before the souls are free. The "care and nourishment" are the fire and the hymns.
